unit.title: Attend to breakdown in hazardous area

summary: This unit prepares you to respond to electrical breakdowns where flammable gas, vapour or dust may be in the air: fuel stations and depots, LPG plants, rum distilleries, sugar factories, mills and sewage pumping stations. You will learn how areas are classified into zones, how to read Ex equipment markings, how the main types of protection work, and how to plan, isolate, gas-test, repair, inspect and hand back equipment under a permit to work, without creating a source of ignition.

blocks.p: In most places a fault on a light or a motor is an inconvenience. In a hazardous area it can be the start of an explosion. A spark from opening a live terminal box, a hot lamp, a dropped tool, an uncertified gland or a missing cover bolt can ignite a flammable atmosphere and kill people and destroy a plant. This unit is for Level 3 trainees who will attend breakdowns on electrical equipment in such places, as part of a team and often leading it, always under the control of the site's authorised people.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Explain what makes an area hazardous
Describe flammable gases, vapours, mists and dusts, the fire triangle, flash point, explosive limits and vapour density, with Jamaican examples.
Find the zone (or class and division), gas or dust group and temperature class for the place where the breakdown is, from the site's drawing.
Read Ex markings and choose equipment
Decode a marking such as Ex db IIB T4 Gb, and decide whether a replacement suits the place where it will be fitted.
Explain the main types of protection
Say how flameproof, increased safety, intrinsic safety and dust protection prevent ignition, and what must never be changed on each.
Plan the job, obtain a permit to work, follow its conditions, and stop and suspend it when conditions change.
Isolate electrically and from the process, prove dead safely, wait for hot parts to cool, and control static, tools, phones and hot work.
Check the detector, test in the right places before and during the work, and act on the readings and alarms.
Diagnose safely, repair like for like with certified parts, and look after flamepaths, glands, plugs, terminals and IS circuits.
Close it correctly, have it inspected and recorded, hand back the permit and restore the supply through the authorised person.
Brief and supervise the team, keep untrained people out of the zone, write the breakdown report and update the equipment register.

head: Workplace
What can form an explosive atmosphere
rows: Fuel service stations, fuel depots and terminals, the oil refinery
Petrol vapour around dispensers, tanks, vents, tanker unloading points and pits; diesel mist where it sprays
LPG (propane and butane) from leaks at pumps, compressors, filling heads and valves
Alcohol vapour in still houses, spirit stores, filling and blending areas
Sugar dust in bagging, conveying and storage; also fuels and bagasse dust
Grain and flour dust in silos, elevators, mills and bagging
Sewage pumping stations and treatment works, landfills
Vehicle body shops and factories with spray booths
Power stations and plants using natural gas
Natural gas (mostly methane) at pipework, valves and gas turbines

blocks.note: Only people who are trained, assessed as competent and **authorised by the site** may work on equipment in a hazardous area, and only under the site's permit system. As a trainee, you do this work under the direct supervision of an authorised person. Classroom exercises and training rigs are never connected to a live supply.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A fire or an explosion needs three things together: **fuel** (a flammable gas, vapour, mist or dust), **oxygen** (normally from the air) and a **source of ignition** (a spark, a hot surface or a flame). Take away any one and there is no fire. In a hazardous area, fuel and air may be present at any time, so the only side of the triangle you can control is **ignition**: everything in this unit is about not providing it.

An **explosive atmosphere** is a mixture of a flammable substance with air in which, once it is ignited, the flame spreads through the whole mixture. In an enclosed space the burning gases expand so fast that the pressure can blow apart equipment and buildings.

head: Property
Meaning
Why it matters on a breakdown
rows: Petrol, LPG, alcohol and solvents give off vapour that ignites at normal temperatures.
The lowest temperature at which a liquid gives off enough vapour to be lit by a flame

Below the air temperature, the liquid is always giving off ignitable vapour. Petrol's is about −40 °C; strong spirits' are well below Jamaican air temperatures; diesel's is usually above about 52 °C, so it is less volatile, but its mist or a heated spill can still burn.
The lowest concentration of gas in air that can burn
Below the LEL the mixture is too weak to burn. Gas detectors read in % of LEL.
The highest concentration that can burn
Above it the mixture is too rich, but it becomes explosive again as air gets in, so a rich mixture is never 'safe'.
How heavy the gas is compared with air
Heavy gases (LPG, petrol vapour) sink and collect in pits, drains and trenches; light gases (methane, hydrogen) rise and collect under roofs.
The temperature at which the mixture ignites on a hot surface, with no spark or flame
Sets how hot equipment surfaces may get: the temperature class.
How small a spark can ignite the mixture
Sets the gas group: hydrogen and acetylene ignite from the tiniest spark.

head: Substance
Explosive range in air, about
Heavier or lighter than air
Notes
rows: Rises; collects under roofs and covers. Gas group IIA, T1.
Sinks and travels along the ground into drains and trenches. Group IIA; propane T1, butane T2.
Flash point far below air temperature. Group IIA, T3.
Ignites very easily. Group IIC, T1.
Strong spirits give off vapour at normal Jamaican temperatures. Take the group and temperature class from the site's drawing.
Explodes as a cloud above a minimum concentration
A layer can smoulder; a disturbed layer makes a cloud.

blocks.note: Figures vary a little between sources; the site's safety data sheets and area classification drawing are the ones to use. Never rely on smell: you get used to it, some gases have little smell, and hydrogen sulphide deadens the sense of smell.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Combustible dust explodes when it is raised into a cloud in a confined space and ignited. A small first explosion often shakes down dust lying on beams, ducts and motors, which forms a much bigger cloud and a far worse second explosion. That is why dust layers must not be allowed to build up, and why dust is never blown off with compressed air. A dust layer on hot equipment can also smoulder and later ignite a cloud.

sections.title: Area classification: zones, divisions and the drawing

blocks.p: A site with flammable materials is studied by competent engineers, who decide where an explosive atmosphere could occur, how often and for how long. The result is the **area classification**, shown on the **area classification drawing** (hazardous area drawing) and kept in the site's records. Before any breakdown work you find the exact spot on this drawing: never guess the zone.

head: Zone
Explosive gas atmosphere is…
Example
rows: Present all the time, or for long periods, or often
Inside a fuel storage tank above the liquid; inside a closed process vessel
Likely to occur now and then in normal operation
Close to a tanker unloading point, a filling head, a tank vent or a pump seal
Not likely in normal operation, and if it does occur it lasts only a short time
The wider area around Zone 1, such as around pumps and pipework that leak only if something fails

head: Zone
Explosive dust cloud is…
Example
rows: Present all the time, or for long periods, or often
Inside a sugar or flour hopper, silo or dust collector
Likely now and then in normal operation
Around bag-filling points and conveyor transfer points
Not likely in normal operation, and only briefly if it occurs
The wider area of a bagging room where dust could escape only if something fails

blocks.p: Anywhere not classified is a **non-hazardous (safe) area**. Zones are three-dimensional: a zone may extend a set distance around and above a source, or to floor level and along trenches for heavy gases.

Some sites, especially those built to North American codes (and Jamaica's electrical code is based on the US NEC), mark hazardous areas by **class and division** instead of zones. The NEC allows both systems.

head: Class and division
Meaning
Roughly like
rows: Easily ignited fibres and flyings, such as cotton lint
Hazard present in normal operation, or likely
Hazard present only in abnormal conditions, such as a leak or failure

blocks.p: Under the class system, gases are put into Groups A, B, C and D (A and B are the most easily ignited, like IIC; C is like IIB; D, which includes petrol and LPG, is like IIA). Equipment certified for zones and equipment certified for divisions are marked differently. Never assume they are interchangeable: check the drawing, the marking and the certificate, and ask the authorised person.

ul: The boundaries of each zone, in plan and often in section, with heights and distances.
The gas or dust group the equipment must suit.
The temperature class (or maximum surface temperature for dust) the equipment must meet.
Notes on ventilation or other conditions the classification depends on.

blocks.note: The classification assumes the plant is working as designed, including its ventilation. If an extract fan fails, a cover is left off a tank, or a leak is found, the hazard may be bigger than the drawing shows. Stop and tell the person in charge.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Every site with hazardous areas should keep a **hazardous area equipment register** or **dossier**: the area classification drawings, and for each item of Ex equipment its location, type of protection, marking, certificate, installation records and inspection history. Before attending a breakdown you look the item up here, so you know exactly what is fitted and can bring the right certified spares. After the repair you update it, so it shows what is now installed.

sections.title: Ex equipment: markings and types of protection

blocks.p: Electrical equipment for hazardous areas is designed and **certified** so that it cannot ignite the atmosphere it is made for, provided it is installed and maintained exactly as its certificate says. Its marking tells you where it may be used.
Example: **Ex db IIB T4 Gb**, with a certificate number such as IECEx XXX 21.0123X (the details vary with the certification scheme).

head: Part
Example
Meaning
rows: Certified for explosive atmospheres. Equipment certified under the European ATEX rules also carries a hexagon symbol and a code such as II 2 G.
Flameproof enclosure (d), at level b. Others: e (increased safety), i (intrinsic safety), p (pressurised), m (encapsulated), t (dust protection by enclosure).
Equipment group and gas or dust group
Group II = gases (not mines). IIA, IIB, IIC from least to most easily ignited. Group III = dusts: IIIA fibres, IIIB non-conductive dust, IIIC conductive dust.
The hottest its surface may get: T4 = 135 °C. For dust equipment, a maximum surface temperature is given instead, such as T135 °C.
How well protected it is, which links it to zones: Ga, Gb, Gc for gas; Da, Db, Dc for dust.
An X at the end means special conditions of use are in the certificate: you must read them. A U means it is only a component, to be built into certified equipment.
The air temperatures it is certified for. If none is marked, it is normally −20 °C to +40 °C.

blocks.p: The equipment's maximum surface temperature must be **below the auto-ignition temperature** of the gas. A higher T number is a **cooler** class. So where the drawing asks for T3, equipment marked T3, T4, T5 or T6 may be used; T1 or T2 may not.

blocks.h: The three checks for a replacement

head: Check
Rule
Example: the drawing asks for Zone 1, IIA, T3
rows: Gb or Ga: yes. Gc: no.
The same or higher (IIC covers IIB and IIA; IIB covers IIA)
The same or cooler (a higher T number)
T3, T4, T5, T6: yes. T1, T2: no.

blocks.p: Then check the rest: the ambient range against the real temperature on site, any X conditions on the certificate, the IP rating for weather and washdown, and that it is the right size, rating and fixing for the job.

blocks.note: Jamaican plant rooms, roof spaces, canopies and enclosures in full sun can go well above 40 °C. Equipment marked only for −20 °C to +40 °C must not be used where it will be hotter, unless the maker confirms it is suitable, because its surfaces could then exceed its temperature class. Coastal sites also bring salt air, which corrodes bolts, glands and flamepath faces quickly.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: How the main types of protection work

head: Type
How it prevents ignition
Zones (usually)
Take care during repair
rows: Gas may get inside, but the enclosure is strong enough to contain an explosion. Burning gas escaping through the long, narrow joints (flamepaths) is cooled so it cannot ignite the gas outside.
No damage, paint, sealant or extra gaskets on flamepath faces; every bolt of the right type, tightened as the maker says; certified glands and stopping plugs; no new holes.
No arcs, sparks or hot spots in normal use: good-quality terminals, extra spacing and insulation, and a sealed enclosure (at least IP54) keeping it clean and dry.
Only the certified terminals, the right number and size of conductors per terminal, tightened correctly; nothing extra inside; seals and glands intact.
The energy in the circuit is kept so low, even with faults, that it cannot ignite the gas. A barrier or isolator in the safe area limits the energy.
Keep IS wiring separate; replace like for like; never connect uncertified instruments or devices that add energy.
Clean air or inert gas keeps the enclosure above outside pressure, so gas cannot get in. The supply is cut if the pressure is lost.
Purge before switching on; never defeat the pressure switch.
Sparking or hot parts are sealed in compound.
Dust protection by enclosure, Ex t
Dust-tight enclosure with a limited surface temperature.
Seals, glass and covers intact; keep dust layers off.

blocks.note: Older equipment may be marked Ex n (for example Ex nA, 'non-sparking') for Zone 2. Newer equipment uses Ex ec instead. Treat each according to its marking and certificate.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Permits, authorisation and planning the response

head: Role
What they do
rows: Appointed by the site. Checks the job, the hazards and the zone; arranges isolations and gas testing; issues and cancels permits.
Permit holder (person in charge of the work)
Accepts the permit, briefs the team, keeps the work inside it, and signs it back.
Trained and assessed for hazardous-area work on the types of protection involved, for example through a recognised hazardous-area competence course. Does or directly supervises the work.
Trained to use the detector; tests and records results as the permit says.
Stops and isolates the process, and knows where people are working.

blocks.p: Only authorised people may open, repair or test Ex equipment in a zone, because a mistake that looks harmless, such as a missing bolt or the wrong gland, may cause an explosion weeks later.
A **permit to work** is a written document that allows named, authorised people to do a stated job, at a stated place and time, with stated precautions. Typical contents:

ul: The exact equipment and the work to be done, and its location and zone.
The electrical isolations and the process isolations (valves closed and locked, lines drained or purged), with lock and tag numbers.
The gas test results, the times, who tested, and how often testing must be repeated.
The PPE, the tools and instruments allowed, and any items banned in the zone.
Other permits or certificates that go with it: hot work, confined space entry, electrical isolation certificate.
The times it is valid, and the signatures of the issuer and the holder.
The hand-back section: work done, equipment left safe, isolations to be removed.

blocks.p: If conditions change (a gas alarm, a new leak, ventilation failing, the job turning out bigger than planned), the work stops and the permit is **suspended** until the issuer has reassessed it.

blocks.h: The first steps when a breakdown is reported

flow: Take the report: what failed, where, when, what the operator saw and did
Look the item up in the register: marking, certificate, drawings, history
Check the zone, group and temperature class at that spot on the drawing
Collect matching certified spares, tools and permitted instruments
Report to the person in charge on site, and do not open anything yet
Plan the job with a risk assessment and method statement
Apply for the permit; isolations and gas tests are arranged
Brief the team, then start work within the permit

blocks.note: When a light or motor fails in a classified area, your first step is to report it and arrange a permit, not to open it 'just to look'. Opening a live or hot Ex enclosure in a flammable atmosphere is exactly how explosions are caused.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Check that every member is trained and authorised for the area. Anyone who is not stays outside the classified area (for example fetching parts or keeping records) and is briefed on the emergency plan.

Hold a briefing at the permit point before entry: the job, the zone and hazards, the permit conditions, the isolations, the gas test results and who is testing, PPE, banned items, the escape route and meeting point.
Give each person a clear task, and stay with the team while it works.
Watch that nobody goes beyond the permit, and stop the work if anything changes.

sections.title: Controlling ignition, isolating and gas testing

blocks.h: Sources of ignition and their control

head: Source
Examples on a breakdown
Control
rows: Opening a live enclosure; making or breaking connections; test instruments; switching
Isolate and lock off; prove dead only with instruments the permit allows; certified equipment only
A lamp or motor just switched off; a hot bearing
Wait the time on the warning label before opening; check temperatures
Welding, grinding, cutting, drilling with sparks
Avoid it, or take the item to a workshop outside the zone; otherwise a separate hot work permit, gas-free conditions, continuous testing and a fire watch
A steel tool dropped on concrete or steel; hammering
Carry tools in pouches; work gas-free; use the tools the permit allows
Fuel flowing in hoses; synthetic clothing; plastic sheets
Antistatic footwear and suitable clothing; bond and earth metal items; do not take off clothing layers in the zone
Ordinary phones, radios, torches, cameras, meters
Only items certified for the zone, unless the permit allows them with gas-free conditions
Vans, generators, compressors near the zone
Keep them outside the zone, as the site rules say

ul: Isolate every live conductor of the circuit, **including the neutral**, at a point outside the hazardous area where possible, and lock and tag it.
Check for other sources: a second supply, a standby generator, a UPS, control circuits fed from another board, and capacitors.

Prove dead. A test instrument can itself make a spark, so prove dead only with an instrument the permit allows (one certified for the zone, or any approved tester once gas-free conditions are confirmed), checked on a proving unit before and after use.

Many Ex enclosures carry a label such as 'After de-energising, delay X minutes before opening'. **Wait that time** so that hot parts cool and capacitors discharge. Some also say 'Do not open when an explosive atmosphere may be present'.

blocks.p: Many breakdowns are on pumps, compressors and valves that carry the flammable material itself. The permit may require **process isolation** as well: the operator stops the plant, closes and locks valves on both sides, drains and vents the line, and may purge it with nitrogen or water. Electrical isolation alone does not stop fuel spraying out when a pump is opened.

head: Sensor
Measures
Watch out for
rows: Needs normal oxygen to read correctly: in a low-oxygen space it can read falsely low. Can be 'poisoned' by silicones and some other chemicals.
Alarms are commonly set at about 19.5% (low) and 23.5% (high); follow the site's settings.
Hydrogen sulphide is toxic at low levels and deadens the sense of smell.

ul: It must be the right type for the gases on site, and within its **calibration** date (calibration is done at the interval the maker or site sets).
**Bump test** it each day before use, with a known test gas, to prove that the sensors respond and the alarms work.
The battery must be charged for the whole job, and the detector itself must be certified for use in the zone.
Test before the permit is issued, and then continuously or at the times the permit sets, while work goes on.

Test where the gas will be: **low** down in pits, drains, trenches and at floor level for heavy gases such as LPG and petrol vapour; **high** up under roofs and covers for light gases such as methane; and at several heights when gases of different weights may be present.
Test around the equipment, inside enclosures before work in them, and anywhere the work will make sparks or heat.
Write the results on the permit with the time and the tester's name.

blocks.p: **10% LEL** means the gas is at one tenth of the lowest concentration that can burn. For a gas with an LEL of 2% by volume, 10% LEL is 0.2% of the air. Sites set the level at which work may start or must stop on the permit; many use 10% LEL or less, with a lower limit (often near zero) for hot work. Any reading above zero means gas is getting out from somewhere: find out why.

blocks.note: If the detector alarms at any time: stop work, make the job safe only if it can be done in seconds without creating a spark, and leave by the agreed escape route to the meeting point, following the site's emergency plan. Do not switch electrical equipment on or off on your way out, and do not go back until the authorised person says it is safe.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Welding, cutting and grinding in a hazardous area are a last resort. Where possible, remove the item and repair it in a workshop outside the zone, or use a bolted or clamped repair instead. If hot work cannot be avoided it needs a separate **hot work permit**, with the area made gas-free, flammable materials removed or covered, continuous gas testing before and during the work, fire extinguishers and a fire watch who stays on after the work finishes.

Wet wells, tanks, pits and silos are often **confined spaces** as well as hazardous areas. Entry needs a confined-space permit, testing for flammable gas, oxygen and toxic gas before and during entry, forced ventilation, a trained standby person outside, and a rescue plan and equipment ready before anyone goes in.

sections.title: Finding the fault and repairing Ex equipment

ul: Ask the operator what happened, and look at the records: is this a repeat fault?
Look from outside first: damage, missing bolts, water, corrosion, a damaged cable or gland, a broken glass, a dust layer, signs of overheating.
Check what the protection did: an overload trip, an earth-leakage trip, a blown fuse. Each points to different causes.

Do not keep resetting a tripped motor or circuit to keep the plant running. Repeated resets can turn a small fault into a burnt winding, a flashover inside the enclosure, or a hot surface in the zone. Find the cause first.
Do the tests the permit allows, with the instruments it allows.

head: What you find
Likely causes
What to do
rows: Water inside a terminal box or fitting; earth-leakage trips
Damaged gland seal, cracked or perished cover gasket, missing plug, loose cover, flooding after heavy rain
Dry and inspect; replace seals, glands or plugs with certified parts; find how water got in; insulation test only if the permit allows
Seized pump or bearing, low voltage, single phasing on a three-phase motor, wrong overload setting
Check the mechanical side with the fitter; check supply voltages; never raise the overload setting to stop the trips
Failed lamp or driver, loose connection, water inside, damaged cable
Replace like for like with the maker's parts
Isolate it and keep it out of service until repaired with the maker's parts or replaced
IS loop reading zero or full scale
Open or shorted field wiring, failed transmitter, failed barrier or isolator, poor IS earth
Check with certified instruments; replace like for like; check the IS earth
Poor housekeeping, damaged seals on conveyors and hoppers
Clean with an approved vacuum; report the dust source

ul: **Like for like.** A replacement must have a suitable type of protection and protection level for the zone, a gas group the same or higher, and a temperature class the same or cooler, and must be certified. Check its ambient range and certificate conditions too.

**No modifications.** Never drill extra holes, cut, weld, file, repaint machined faces, change internal parts or fit extra components in certified equipment. Any change outside the certificate makes it uncertified, and may weaken the enclosure.
**Certified parts only.** Lamps, drivers, glasses, seals, glands, plugs and bolts as the maker specifies.

**Major repairs** (rewinding an Ex motor, machining flamepaths) are done only by the maker or a specialist repair workshop working to the repair standard, and the item is marked to show it has been repaired.

**If the right spare is not available**, the equipment stays isolated. Tell the person in charge and agree a safe temporary plan, such as a standby pump. Losing production costs money; an explosion costs lives.
The **flamepath** is the long, narrow gap between machined faces (on the cover and body, around shafts and in threaded joints). It cools burning gas escaping from an internal explosion.
Inspect the faces for scratches, pitting, rust and damage. Damaged faces are not filed or polished: the part is replaced as the maker says.

Clean the faces only as the maker allows. Never paint them, never put sealant or silicone on them, and never fit a gasket the maker did not design in. Protect them against rust only with the non-setting grease the maker approves.
Where the maker gives a maximum gap, check it with feeler gauges.
Keep the outlets of flanged flamepaths clear of nearby walls, pipes, brackets and steelwork, as the installation rules require.
Threaded covers and entries need enough threads engaged (commonly at least five full threads); never force a cross-threaded cover.

blocks.h: Cable glands, entries and stopping plugs

ul: Use only a **certified gland** suited to the enclosure's protection type and to the cable (size, type, armour). Ordinary IP-rated glands are not acceptable.
Where the rules require it, a **barrier gland** filled with setting compound stops gas passing along inside the cable into a flameproof enclosure. Mix and fill it exactly as the maker says.

Close every unused entry with a **certified stopping (blanking) plug** of the right type and thread. Plastic transit caps, tape and ordinary plugs give no protection. Do not fit a stopping plug into a thread adaptor.
Tighten glands and plugs as the maker says, with seals in place.
Connect only to the certified terminals, with the number and size of conductors each terminal is certified for, tightened to the maker's figure.
Fit nothing extra inside: no connector blocks, no spare lengths of cable coiled up, no tools left behind.
Keep the enclosure sealed: cover gasket, glands and plugs intact, so that it stays clean and dry.

IS circuits are kept **separate** from all other circuits: separate cables, separate terminals spaced well apart, often light-blue cable and terminals, so that a fault cannot push extra energy into them.
An IS loop is certified as a **system**: the field device, the cable and the barrier or isolator together. Replace each part like for like, or only with a part the loop documents show is suitable.
A **zener barrier** limits energy by diverting fault current to earth, so it needs a sound, low-resistance IS earth connection. A loose barrier earth is a serious defect.
Use only test instruments certified for IS circuits, or work under a permit with gas-free conditions confirmed. An ordinary meter can add energy, store it, or make a spark as it is connected.
Site rules may allow some work on live IS circuits, because their energy is limited. Follow those rules exactly; they never apply to other types of protection.

blocks.p: An insulation resistance tester produces a high voltage (often 500 V DC) and can make sparks, and a charged cable can spark when touched. Insulation tests in a hazardous area are done only when the permit allows them, normally with gas-free conditions confirmed by a test first. IS circuits are not insulation-tested unless the IS rules and the permit allow it, with barriers and devices disconnected as required.

sections.title: Closing up, return to service, emergencies and records

flow: Remove all tools, off-cuts, loose screws and rags from inside
Check terminations: right terminals, tight, correctly identified
Inspect flamepath faces, seals and gaskets; check gaps if required
Check every gland is certified and tight, and every unused entry is plugged
Refit every cover bolt, of the type the maker specifies, tightened evenly as the maker says
Check the marking is still readable and any glass or guard is intact
Record the inspection and the parts fitted

blocks.note: A flameproof cover with one bolt missing is not 'nearly' flameproof. In an internal explosion the joint can spring open at the gap and let the flame out. Every bolt must be fitted, of the correct type and grade: never a shorter, longer or ordinary bolt.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Before the equipment goes back into service, a competent person carries out a recorded **inspection** of the Ex features that were disturbed (normally a detailed inspection of those parts), and the result is recorded.
The permit holder signs the permit back: work complete, equipment safe, team and tools clear.
The **authorised person** removes the isolations and restores the supply and the process, in a controlled order, and a function test is done.
Watch the equipment run for a time, and check that the fault has not returned.

head: Event
What the team does
rows: Gas alarm or a smell of gas
Stop work; leave by the agreed route to the meeting point; follow the site's emergency plan; report to the control room.
Raise the alarm; leave; fight it only if trained, the fire is small and your escape is clear; call 110 if the site plan says so.
Injury or collapse in a confined space
Raise the alarm and start the rescue plan from outside. Do not enter without breathing apparatus and a rescue team: many deaths are of rescuers.
Isolate the supply without touching the casualty; call for help; first aid.
Stop work, make safe, leave if needed, and tell the permit issuer. The permit is suspended.

blocks.p: Hazardous-area work is only as safe as its records. After the breakdown:

ul: **The breakdown report:** date and time; the equipment and its location and zone; the fault found and its cause; the parts fitted, with their Ex marking and certificate numbers; tests and their results; the inspection done and by whom; the time out of service; and any recommendations (for example, better seals, a different gland, more frequent inspection).
**The equipment register (dossier):** updated to show what is now fitted and its certificate, and the inspection.
**The permit:** signed back and filed.
**Defects** you could not fix are reported in writing to the person in charge, and the equipment is left isolated and labelled.

blocks.note: As team leader, check the equipment yourself before it is closed, make sure the inspection is recorded, sign the permit back, and report to the authorised person before you leave site.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can explain the fire triangle and what an explosive atmosphere is.
I can explain flash point, LEL, UEL, vapour density and auto-ignition temperature, and why each matters.
I can name Jamaican workplaces with hazardous areas and the substances involved.
I can describe Zones 0, 1, 2, 20, 21 and 22, and classes and divisions.
I can find the zone, group and temperature class for a spot on the area classification drawing.
I can decode an Ex marking and match the equipment protection level to the zone.
I can decide whether a replacement suits a place: protection level, gas group, temperature class, ambient range.
I can explain how Ex d, Ex e, Ex i, Ex p and Ex t protection work.
I can explain what a permit to work contains and when it is suspended.
I can list the sources of ignition on a breakdown and how each is controlled.
I can describe electrical and process isolation, proving dead and waiting times.
I can check a gas detector and say where and when to test, and what % LEL means.
I can diagnose a breakdown safely without repeatedly resetting protection.
I can describe the rules for repairs: like for like, no modifications, certified parts.
I can look after flamepaths, glands, stopping plugs, Ex e terminals and IS circuits correctly.
I can close an Ex enclosure correctly and describe how it is returned to service.
I can act in a gas alarm or other emergency.
I can brief and supervise a team, and write the breakdown report and register update.

terms: Area classification drawing
The site's drawing showing hazardous zones, with the gas or dust group and temperature class needed.
Authorised person
Someone appointed by the site to control hazardous work, issue permits and arrange isolations.
Auto-ignition temperature
The temperature at which a flammable mixture ignites on a hot surface without a spark or flame.
Barrier gland
A cable gland filled with setting compound, which stops gas passing along inside the cable.
Bump test
A daily check with a known gas that a detector's sensors respond and its alarms work.
Equipment protection level (EPL)
The level of protection of Ex equipment (Ga, Gb, Gc; Da, Db, Dc), linked to the zones it may be used in.
Equipment register (dossier)
The site's record of its hazardous areas and of every item of Ex equipment, its certificate and inspections.
Ex marking
The marking showing that equipment is certified for explosive atmospheres, and for which.
Flameproof (Ex d)
Protection by an enclosure that contains an internal explosion and cools gases escaping through its joints.
Flamepath
The narrow gap between machined faces of a flameproof joint, which cools escaping burning gas.
Flash point
The lowest temperature at which a liquid gives off enough vapour to be lit by a flame.
Gas group
IIA, IIB or IIC, from least to most easily ignited gases; IIC equipment may be used for all three.
Hazardous area
A place where a flammable gas, vapour, mist or dust may be present in amounts needing special precautions.
Hot work
Work that produces flames, sparks or heat, such as welding, cutting and grinding.
Increased safety (Ex e)
Protection by design that prevents arcs, sparks and hot spots.
Intrinsic safety (Ex i)
Protection by limiting a circuit's energy so it cannot ignite the atmosphere, even with faults.
LEL (lower explosive limit)
The lowest concentration of a gas in air that can burn.
Permit to work
A written document allowing named, authorised people to do stated work at a stated time with stated precautions.
Process isolation
Stopping, isolating, draining and purging the plant so the flammable material cannot reach the work.
Stopping plug
A certified plug that closes an unused cable entry in Ex equipment.
Temperature class
T1 to T6: the highest surface temperature equipment may reach; T6 is the coolest.
Zone
A category of hazardous area based on how often and how long an explosive atmosphere is present.

c1.title: A tripped compressor at a St Catherine LPG plant
c1.text: At an LPG cylinder-filling plant in St Catherine, the motor of the transfer compressor has tripped, and the operator has reset it twice. The area classification drawing shows the compressor house as Zone 1, needing equipment for gas group IIA and temperature class T2. Level 3 technician Andrea Lewis attends under the site's permit system. The stores hold four spare motors of the right size: Ex db IIB T4 Gb; Ex ec IIC T4 Gc; Ex db IIA T1 Gb; and a standard IP55 motor. Inside the faulty motor's Ex eb terminal box, she later finds two cores joined with a screw connector block.

c2.title: Water in a junction box at a Bull Bay pumping station
c2.text: At a sewage pumping station in Bull Bay, St Andrew, the pump keeps tripping on earth leakage. The drawing shows the wet well as Zone 1 and the area just above its opening as Zone 2. Technician Garth Morrison finds water inside an Ex e junction box on the wet-well wall, below a damaged cable gland and a cracked cover gasket. The box can be reached only by climbing down into the wet well. The sewage gives off methane and hydrogen sulphide.

c3.title: A cracked light at a Westmoreland sugar factory
c3.text: During the crop, a sugar factory in Westmoreland calls you to its bagging plant. A light fitting marked Ex tb IIIB T135 °C Db has a cracked glass after a bag struck it. The drawing shows the area round the bagging machines as Zone 22 and the inside of the sugar hopper as Zone 20. A layer of sugar dust about 10 mm thick lies on top of a nearby conveyor motor, and a worker is about to blow it off with compressed air.

c4.title: A dead level reading at a Rockfort fuel depot
c4.text: At a fuel depot in Rockfort, Kingston, the level reading from petrol tank 4 shows zero in the control room. The transmitter on the tank roof is marked Ex ia IIB T4 Ga and is wired in light-blue cable to a zener barrier in a panel in the safe-area control room. Technician Paul suggests checking the loop at the tank with his ordinary multimeter. The spare barrier in the panel drawer is a different model from the one fitted, and the fitted barrier's earth wire is found loose.

c5.title: A light fitting in a Trelawny spirit store
c5.text: Karlene, a Level 3 technician, leads a team replacing a failed flameproof light fitting in the spirit store of a rum distillery in Trelawny. The drawing shows the store as Zone 1, and the store reaches about 45 °C on hot afternoons. The only matching fitting in stores is marked for an ambient range of −20 °C to +40 °C. Because the old fitting had rusted, one of her team suggests a thin bead of silicone on the flamepath to keep water out. Halfway through the job, the store's extract fan stops.

questions.q: Which spare motor may replace the compressor motor, if its size and rating match?
o: Ex ec IIC T4 Gc
Ex db IIA T1 Gb
Ex db IIB T4 Gb
The standard IP55 motor
questions.why: Gb equipment suits Zones 1 and 2; group IIB also covers IIA gases; and T4 (135 °C) is cooler than the T2 (300 °C) the area needs. The Gc motor is for Zone 2 only, the T1 motor may run hotter (up to 450 °C) than T2 allows, and an IP55 motor has no explosion protection at all.

questions.q: Where should the gas tester take readings around the compressor before work starts?
o: Low down: floor level, trenches, pits and drains
At head height, where the workers will breathe the air
Up near the roof, where any escaping gas would collect
Only at the terminal box, where the work will be done
questions.why: LPG is about one and a half to two times as heavy as air, so it sinks and collects in low places such as cable trenches, pits and drains, and can travel a long way along them. Test there and around the equipment. Lighter gases such as methane or hydrogen are tested high up as well.

questions.q: Before work starts, the detector shows 15% LEL beside the compressor. The permit allows work only below 10% LEL. What should happen?
o: Start, as 15% LEL is far too weak to burn
Start, but use only non-sparking hand tools
Retest a metre higher, where it reads lower
No work: find the leak, ventilate, retest
questions.why: 15% LEL means the gas is at 15% of the lowest concentration that can burn: something is leaking, and the level may rise. Work does not start until the cause is found and made safe and a new test shows a level the permit allows. Moving the detector to get a better number defeats the test, and non-sparking tools do not make a gassy area safe.

questions.q: What should Andrea do about the screw connector block inside the Ex eb terminal box?
o: Tape over it well, so that it cannot spark against the box
Remove it; use only the box's certified terminals
Leave it, as the box itself is certified for Zone 1
Swap it for a bigger connector block of the same type
questions.why: Increased safety depends on certified terminals, correct spacing and correct tightening, so that no spark or hot spot can occur. An uncertified connector can loosen, heat up or arc, and it breaks the box's certificate. Every joint must use terminals the certificate allows, tightened to the maker's figure.

questions.q: Why must Garth's detector measure oxygen and hydrogen sulphide as well as flammable gas?
o: An LEL sensor works only when hydrogen sulphide is also present
Toxic H2S and low oxygen kill, and an LEL sensor detects neither
The O2 and H2S readings are needed to convert % LEL into % volume
The permit needs several readings so an average can be worked out
questions.why: A flammable-gas sensor tells you nothing about poison or suffocation. H2S is toxic at low levels and deadens the sense of smell, and a wet well can be short of oxygen. A catalytic LEL sensor also needs oxygen to read correctly, so low oxygen can make it read falsely low.

questions.q: Methane is lighter than air and hydrogen sulphide a little heavier. Where should the wet well be tested before entry?
o: Only at the top, since methane rises out of the well
Only at the bottom, since sewage gases are all heavy
At the hatch only, since the box is near the opening
At the top, middle and bottom, from outside
questions.why: Gases of different weights form layers at different heights, so the well is tested at the top, middle and bottom from outside, before anyone enters, and then continuously while anyone is inside. A test at one level can miss a dangerous layer.

questions.q: To reach the box, Garth must climb down into the wet well. What does this need, besides the electrical and gas controls?
o: A confined-space permit, ventilation, a standby and a rescue plan
Only a second gas test, taken after he reaches the bottom of the well
A dust mask and gloves, as the work is short and near the hatch
Nothing extra, as the electrical permit already covers the well
questions.why: A wet well is a confined space: gas builds up and escape is hard. Entry needs its own permit, testing before and during entry, forced ventilation, a trained person standing by outside, and a rescue plan and equipment ready. Many confined-space deaths are of untrained would-be rescuers.

questions.q: Why does water inside the Ex e box matter for explosion protection, and not just because it trips the pump?
o: Water stops the box's flameproof joints from cooling escaping gas
Water raises the box's temperature class from T4 to a hotter T1
Ex e needs clean, dry insulation; water can track and spark
Water inside only matters in Zone 0, not in Zones 1 and 2
questions.why: Increased safety works by preventing sparks and hot spots: good terminals, spacing and insulation, kept clean and dry by a sealed enclosure (at least IP54). Water and dirt let current track across insulation and arc. Replace the gland and gasket with certified parts and find out how the water got in.

questions.q: What should happen to the light fitting with the cracked glass?
o: Leave it on until the end of the crop, as the crack is small
Seal the crack with clear tape and silicone, then switch on
Fit any glass of the same size from the stores and switch on
Isolate it until the maker's own glass part is fitted
questions.why: The glass is part of the enclosure that keeps dust out and protects the lamp. A cracked glass breaks that protection, so the fitting is isolated and stays off until it is repaired with the maker's part and inspected. Tape, sealant or a glass of unknown type would not restore its certification.

questions.q: What should you tell the worker who is about to blow the dust off the motor?
o: Go ahead, as long as the conveyor motor is switched off first
Stop: it raises a dust cloud; vacuum with an approved cleaner
Go ahead, but only during the lunch break, when it is quiet
Go ahead, since dust only explodes inside the hopper (Zone 20)
questions.why: Compressed air lifts a layer into a cloud, which is exactly what a dust explosion needs, and a small first explosion can raise more dust for a far bigger second one. Remove dust with a vacuum cleaner approved for combustible dust, or as the site's rules say, and do not let layers build up.

questions.q: Why is the 10 mm dust layer on the motor dangerous even if no cloud forms?
o: It makes the motor's marking hard to read during inspection
It adds weight, which overloads the motor's bearings
It traps heat; the motor runs hot and it may smoulder
It is dangerous only if it gets wet and starts to ferment
questions.why: A dust layer acts like a blanket: the motor surface gets hotter, and a thick layer can start to smoulder at a much lower temperature than a cloud ignites. A smouldering layer can later light a dust cloud. Equipment temperatures are chosen assuming layers are kept thin, so housekeeping is part of the protection.

questions.q: What is the lowest equipment protection level allowed in the Zone 22 area round the bagging machines?
o: Dc
Db
Da
Gc
questions.why: Dust Zones 20, 21 and 22 need Da, Db (or Da) and Dc (or better) respectively, so Dc is the minimum in Zone 22. The fitting marked Db is better than the minimum, which is allowed. Gc is a gas level and says nothing about dust.

questions.q: Why must Paul not connect his ordinary multimeter to the transmitter circuit on the tank roof?
o: It is not certified, and could add energy or spark in the zone
It would read the IS loop's current far too high and blow its fuse
The light-blue cable cannot carry the meter's test current
Ordinary meters are made only for 110 V and 220 V circuits
questions.why: An IS circuit is safe because its energy is limited by design. An uncertified instrument can store energy, add its own (on its resistance ranges) or spark as it is connected, in a place where petrol vapour may be present. Use an instrument certified for the zone, or work under a permit with gas-free conditions confirmed.

questions.q: Can the different model of barrier in the drawer replace the fitted one?
o: Yes, if it clips onto the same DIN rail and terminals
Yes, since all zener barriers do exactly the same job
Only if the loop's IS documents show it matches
No; a barrier may never be replaced once it is installed
questions.why: An IS loop is certified as a system: the barrier's output must suit the field device and the cable. A barrier with different ratings could let too much energy into the hazardous area. Replace like for like, or with one the loop documents show is suitable, and record it.

questions.q: Why does the barrier's loose earth wire matter?
o: It makes the level reading drift by a few per cent each day
Its earth only matters during lightning, which is rare
It stops the barrier's indicator lamp from lighting up
The barrier needs its earth to divert fault energy safely
questions.why: A zener barrier limits the voltage reaching the field by passing fault current to earth. Without a sound, low-resistance IS earth, a fault on the safe-area side could send dangerous energy along the cable to the tank. Treat it as a defect: remake and check the connection under the permit, and record it.

questions.q: Can the fitting from stores be used in the spirit store?
o: Yes, as its temperature class already allows for the heat
Not unless the maker approves it for a 45 °C store
Yes, as Ta ratings matter only for equipment used outdoors
Yes, if it is switched off on the hottest afternoons
questions.why: Ex equipment is certified for a stated ambient range, normally −20 °C to +40 °C unless marked otherwise. Above it, surfaces may exceed the temperature class. In hot Jamaican stores and plant rooms, check the marked range against the real temperature and get the maker's confirmation or a fitting rated for it.

questions.q: What should Karlene say about putting silicone on the flamepath?
o: No; only the maker's approved grease, never sealant
Yes: it keeps out water, so the fitting lasts longer
Yes, as long as the bead is under 1 mm thick
Yes, if the flamepath faces are painted first
questions.why: A flamepath works by being a precise, narrow gap that cools escaping flame. Sealant, paint or an extra gasket can change the gap or hold the faces apart. Protect the faces against rust only with the non-setting grease or treatment the maker allows, and replace corroded parts.

questions.q: What should the team do when the extract fan stops halfway through the job?
o: Finish quickly, before any vapour can build up
Open the doors wider and carry on as planned
Stop, make safe, leave and tell the issuer
Carry on, as the gas detector has not alarmed yet
questions.why: The zones on the drawing assume the ventilation is working. Without it, vapour can build up beyond what the permit allowed for. Conditions have changed, so work stops, the permit is suspended, and work restarts only when the issuer has reassessed it.

questions.q: A gas has an auto-ignition temperature of 210 °C. Which equipment temperature classes may be used where it is present?
o: T1, T2 or T3
T4, T5 or T6 only
T1 or T2 only
T3, T4, T5 or T6
questions.why: The equipment's maximum surface temperature must stay below 210 °C. T3 allows up to 200 °C, and T4, T5 and T6 are cooler still, so all four may be used. T2 (300 °C) and T1 (450 °C) could ignite the gas.

questions.q: A site built to North American practice marks an area 'Class I, Division 2'. What does this mean?
o: Combustible dust is present for long periods in normal use
Flammable gas may be there, but not in normal operation
Flammable gas is present all the time, as inside a tank
The area is safe, as Division 2 is not a hazardous area
questions.why: Class I covers flammable gases and vapours. Division 2 is where they are present only in abnormal conditions, such as a leak, roughly like Zone 2. Division 1 is where they are likely in normal operation (roughly Zones 0 and 1). Class II covers combustible dusts.
